name: Denton
classification_notes: Bold, tightly kerned serif titling drawn from 1970s design references places this as a display-leaning titling serif with a dedicated text cut.
summary: A warm, tightly kerned titling serif reviving 1970s headline design, with condensed and text cuts for range.
description: Denton takes the bold, tightly kerned serif titling common in 1970s design and updates it for contemporary use, running to 86 fonts across weight and width variables. Condensed and extra-condensed widths sit alongside a dedicated Text subfamily, all with true italics rather than sloped romans. Built for warmth and personality rather than neutral utility.
foundry_blurb: Peregrin Studio describes Denton as full of warmth, bringing expressive 70s-era design into the 21st century through tight kerning, uniform rhythm and carefully considered letter interaction.

name: Systemia
classification_notes: A Swiss neo-grotesque structure crossed with technical monospace references such as OCR-B places this as a grotesque with a technical inflection.
summary: A Swiss neo-grotesque crossed with monospace technical references, channelling 1980s technology design.
description: Systemia combines the finesse of the classic Swiss neo-grotesque genre with the clarity of monospace typefaces, referencing Mercator, Akzidenz-Grotesk and OCR-B. Easily distinguishable characters and a mix of curved and sharp stems give it a technical yet refined aesthetic suited to systems-driven branding.
foundry_blurb: Peregrin Studio describes Systemia as combining the finesse of the classic Swiss grotesk genre with the clarity and technical appeal of monospace typefaces, drawing on 1980s technology design.

name: Ashcroft
classification_notes: Sitting between sans and serif with flared stroke endings, referencing carved British civic lettering, this is classified as a flared serif.
summary: A flared serif drawing on carved Portland stone lettering and British Underground signage.
description: Ashcroft dances between sans and serif forms, its flared stroke endings referencing early 20th-century British lettering: carved stone names, Underground signage, and bronze civic inscriptions. The result balances a tactile, handmade tension with practical, contemporary use. One of Peregrin Studio's newest releases.
foundry_blurb: Peregrin Studio describes Ashcroft as balancing carved form with human warmth, bringing a tactile, handmade tension to a typeface fit for modern use, sitting as a flared serif dancing between sans and serif forms.
